evidence.text: I think it's a cool idea, and I applaud you guys at such a young age for pursuing it. For me, it's a simple decision, because I don't invest in pre-revenue companies. So I'm going to pass. But keep up the good work. You guys are onto something.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Hello, my name is Troy Pettie.

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: And I'm Evan Thomas.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Our company is Guru Games. So growing up in Las Vegas, Evan and I were constantly surrounded by casinos and their games. But as we got closer to turning 21, we realized that there weren't any games that either of us wanted to play. After some research we realized that this isn't just our problem. This is a problem plaguing the entire gaming industry. Nobody can find a way to attract the newest generation of gamers to gamble in their casinos playing their games. So to solve this problem, Evan and I founded Guru Games.

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: We're currently raising $600,000 to develop our team as well as cover the legal costs with running a for-real-money gambling studio. And that's our one minute pitch.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Alright. Very good!

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So, tell us a bit about your background.

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: So we're both UNLV engineering students. UNLV is University of Nevada Las Vegas, if none of you guys are familiar. So I actually started my first semester of college at Air Force Academy. During that first semester I learned that the military wasn't where I wanted to put my resources towards. I really kind of fell in love with entrepreneurship and creating my own ideas. So I took that to UNLV. Me and Troy took a gaming innovation class. The person who ran that class, he was basically our personal mentor. He taught us everything we know about games. If you look in a casino right now, slot machines are just traditional spinning wheels, and you get a payout. There's no interaction. Millennials are turned off by it.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Troy, we do want to hear about your background, too.

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: Yeah, go ahead and tell your background, Troy.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: So, my background is pretty much the same, except that I didn't really get into the startup world until we took that class.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: You're starting your own... So, you're going to partner with casinos? Or you're going to start your own casino?

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: So, exactly. We are partnering not so much with casinos. So I'll just give a quick background on how the gaming industry works. You have your casino operators who are like MGM, Caesars.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: What happens is we'll actually design the entire theme and the sound and basically all the graphics, the experience of the cabinet. And then they'll just manufacture it. So all the design, all the creative control of the game, falls underneath us, but they're just our distributor. They're our big partner that's going to get us actually into the casinos.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: And your manufacturing partner.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Yes, exactly.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: So manufacturing and distributing partner.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: What does the revenue stream look like? How does the split work and how much money would you expect to...?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: So the split, kind of... It changes from company to company. It all has to be negotiated.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: But what's the range? Give us an idea.

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: Typical deals look like a 70-30 or a 60-40 split. Some can go as high as 80-20 and some can go as low as 50-50 in terms of...

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So have you created the software already? Have you created the game?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: You've created the game.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: So you guys are game developers?

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Both of you?

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Yep.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Are you both still at UNLV?

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: We're only 20. We're only 20.

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: We're both still students there.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: So yeah. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: So you can't even play your game?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: This is illegal. Are we engaging in illegal activity right now?

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: We're contributing to delinquency of a minor.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: So. How many of you guys have played slot machines?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: All of us.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: All of you guys. Okay.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: I'm really good at them.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And Howie's really good at them.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: I'm a good slot player.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: You're a good slot player?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Are you?

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: I mean, that's what Howie's job is, basically, right? You just randomly pick and just see what happens.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: What? My investment thesis?

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Yeah, of course.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: So, you've all played slots. So you all have gotten some near misses, to where you wish you could just kind of flip it and get it to actually line up on the line, you know, and get paid for it.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Absolutely.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Too many times you get two sevens and then you miss it by like a millimeter. We made a game, right, that... Sorry. We made a game that is completely math verified, but allows you to completely control how you make your lines. So let me give you an example…

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: And now you've got this diagonal of bars, and this right here, this line of cherries. And then you can also get this. Right. And now you've got a little horizontal of bells. So finish. Right. And you won $7.50 from that win. So when it comes to slot machines you can choose things and what not. But you can't actually affect your wager. This game, you can mess up on and affect your wager. This game, you can maximize your payout if given a good board.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: One thing I'm concerned about is casinos are always focused on velocity of gambling.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And it seems like this would slow down the velocity.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Amazingly enough, for people, the learning curve for this game is very similar to that of video poker. So if any of you play video poker, you're kind of slow at first, you kind of learn, like, oh it's better to hold a pair than a high card, right? And then eventually you get to the point where you can play 400 rounds an hour. Evan and I have been playing this game for around six months, and we can play 320 rounds an hour at almost perfect strategy.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And how does that compare with the regular slot velocity?

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Regular slot velocity is around 450.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So, yeah, that's a significant slowdown after months of your training.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: But the problems is is that you get bored from playing the slot machine.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: So, sure, if you get 500 rounds per hour. But that's if the person plays for the full hour. That's if it's always being played.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So the tradeoff you're saying is this helps them to keep the player there longer, even though they're playing slower?

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Exactly.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: I know a little bit about, I've read a little bit about the psychology behind these game mechanics in casinos, and to Phil's point there is something called the zone. You guys are familiar with the zone?

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Oh yep. You just don't know what you're doing. You just do it.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: It's not even about winning or losing. It's just the mechanics of the game, and the lights and the sound are completely, have been completely calibrated scientifically to make sure that you sit there for hours on end. It seems like, are you saying this enhances the zone? Or can this possibly take you out of the zone? Because there's been years and years of research to get people into this "zone." And now this seems a little bit more interactive.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: You definitely get into the zone playing this game. Once you get used to the mechanic, you definitely get into the zone.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: But how long until you get used to it? Because this is sort of modifying a little bit of human behavior, in terms of this is a new thing, you know. How do you get people to get in?

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: I don't know if it's that new, Howie. I mean this is for people who play social games, right? You play Candy Crush or Bejeweled. It's that mechanic.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: I'm saying people who play slot machines.

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: The zone works for the traditional baby boomer gamblers. That's the bread and butter of the casinos right now. But the casinos are worried about how are they going to attract that new gambler, how are they going to attract that underserved gambler that doesn't currently have a game in the market for them. They don't want to just go and sit mindlessly at a slot machine and get in the zone. They want a more interactive experience. And that's what we're trying to bring to the table.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Essentially this would be what the casino calls 'found money'. Because these people aren't gambling now. So any amount of money that they spend gambling on our game is found money. It's money they wouldn't have made anyway.

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: Right now we're in talks with one of the biggest gaming equipment manufacturers in the country about a distribution deal where, exactly what I was talking about, the studio distributor deal. So, we're in early talks there. And then we've been approached by multiple online casino, online casino, the people that run the online casinos, the operators, in that space.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: So, you're game developers and you have relationships in Vegas that can find manufacturing partners and distributors, and they will potentially pay you for your software, for the games that you're developing. I'm curious: why are you raising money?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: The reason we're raising money is because we're basically, we've been bootstrapping this entire time, and we've gotten to the point where we need a bigger team and a full time graphic designer as well as a sound designer, to start working on the full design for this game.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: But you said, if you're working with some of the distributors that you could take a lower split today in exchange for having them do some of the final touches, right?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: Yes. We lose a lot of the creative control in that aspect, and that's one of the things we're really worried about. Because innovation is so stagnant in the gaming industry, we would hate to lose creative control to one of these big manufacturers and then see them tarnish our game into something that we didn't want it to be in the first place.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I still don't understand why you need the money? If you actually created a game which somebody wants, why would you not just license it to them and start creating revenue?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: That's a good question. You want to tackle this one?

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Yeah. We're trying to build a brand. This isn't just a product.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Go ahead answer.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: So what I'm saying is, we want our own team of graphic designers, our own team of sound designers, and for the other ideas that we have and we want to make games that are Guru Games.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Do you think that might be a good idea to try to sell your first one, to bring in some revenue, to support that?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: That's what we're currently, that's what some of the talks that we're having now.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: That's what you're doing?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: Yeah, exactly.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Yeah. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: It's the difference between the game getting on the floor at the beginning of the year or the game getting on the floor in a year and a half.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So the game is not ready to put into casinos yet?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: No, it's not.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Because it's not at the level that you need, correct?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: In order to get it to the level that you need you need to add additional expertise, right?

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Or you get partners on board that can accommodate those?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yes, but he's saying that they lose control that way.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Right. But in the beginning, just to get this thing developed, get it into the casinos, get some money being generated. Maybe just proof of concept. Get it out there.

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: We have a lot of interest from heads of, high up positions, in these casino companies who are begging for innovation.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Well, you can also launch this online. For online casinos, right?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: You would think you could enter that market even easier.

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: And actually the online casinos is actually less work for us. We're approaching online casinos as we speak. But the problem with that is we have to figure out our deal with the big guy first, because we need to see how much of the pie the big guy wants. The big guy might want to say I want social casino, I want online casino, and I want land based casino rights. I want all those distribution channels. So we want to make sure we pleasure that person first, because they're our main source of revenue and land based is the main source of gaming revenue.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: Have you done any like, have you pushed this game out free in the app store?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: Just so someone can... You need data to say that people do sit and play this for three hours or whatever it is. What sort of data do you have on that?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: It's basically, we're not promoting it, it's basically word of mouth around our friends, we’re keeping it small to start. All of the feedback we've gotten from our players so far is this game is addictive. Like, I can't stop playing it, I would love to play this in a casino.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Remind me again what you're raising and the valuation?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: We're raising $600,000 and we are not going for a specific valuation. And then down the road we can talk more specifics about how that convertible note looks.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: How much have you raised?

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: We actually, today is our first day that we're starting fundraising. So we're kicking off with a bang, I guess you would say.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: I like what you're doing . I know that casinos have a huge problem with millennials. And millennials prefer table games, but the table games aren't generally as profitable. And the slots used to be the bread and butter of the casinos and they're sort of dying out, right. So I get that. And I think this is a really interesting solution to that. I would recommend you either sign a deal with a third-party game studio, just license the game out. Or get into one of these online casinos. And not make this one game, like what you're trying to stake your whole business on, like take a haircut on it, but get the revenue through the door, and focus on that as your fundraising. Keep most of the company to yourselves. You don't need to sell a bunch of equity with this kind of business. You have one decent hit and you get your name out in the world with the revenue coming in, and then that second game you hire the full team and then you really build the brand. I don’t think you have to do that on the first game but we need to see some sort of traction first. And so like for that reason, I'm going to pass.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: You have some anecdotal validations with these conversations, which is awesome. Those are great signals. That doesn't happen every day, when these casino heads react the way that they do. And I also think, believe it or not, your age, you should use that to your advantage. There's people that want to help kids. You guys are taking initiative. It's amazing. You're still in college, but you're thinking entrepreneurial. You should leverage that to get people to help you. I think that if you continue to explore this and like get the data, like Jake was saying, put it into casinos, start getting those metrics in terms of time at machine, velocity, all that sort of stuff, then I think that becomes a much more exciting and interesting thing for me to want to get involved in. Because it's like, wow, this is kind of on the bleeding edge of where casino games can go. But for all those reasons right now I'm going to pass, but I'd love to see where it goes and maybe revisit in the future.

turns.speaker: Evan
turns.text: Awesome. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I think it's a cool idea, and I applaud you guys at such a young age for pursuing it. For me, it's a simple decision, because I don't invest in pre-revenue companies. So I'm going to pass. But keep up the good work. You guys are onto something.

turns.speaker: Troy
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.text: So, I have never played Candy Crush. I've never played Bejeweled. I don't know anything about games. I have played a slot machine, that's true.
